workedExamples.stem:
An alkene has three carbon atoms.
(a) Name it. [1]
(b) Give its molecular formula. [1]
(c) Draw its displayed formula. [2]
(d) State what is meant by a functional group, and name the alkenes'. [2]

steps.working: Three carbons gives the prefix prop; a double bond gives the ending -ene. The name is propene.
steps.decision: Count the carbons before you write anything. Summer 2025 records this being answered ethene or but-1-ene, which are two and four carbons.

steps.working: CnH2n with n = 3: 2 × 3 = 6 hydrogens, so C3H6.
steps.decision: No "+2". That belongs to the alkanes, and using it here would give C3H8.

options: Because the second carbon-to-carbon bond uses two bonds that hydrogens would otherwise take
Because alkenes are smaller than alkanes
Because the double bond replaces a carbon
whyMenu.explain: The carbons are the same in number; it is the hydrogens that are two fewer, because the extra C–C bond has used up two bonding positions.

steps.working: Draw three carbons in a row, with a double bond between the first and second.
steps.decision: Chain first, double bond second. Where you put the double bond decides the name, so decide it before the hydrogens.

steps.working: Fill every spare bond with a hydrogen: 2 on the first carbon, 1 on the second, 3 on the third.
steps.decision: Count to four at each carbon. The two doubly-bonded carbons have used two bonds on each other, so they take fewer hydrogens; the total comes to 6, which checks against the formula.

steps.working: A functional group is the reactive group in a molecule; the alkenes' is the carbon-to-carbon double bond, C=C.
steps.decision: Both halves are marks. If the question asks you to circle it, ring the two carbons and the double bond and leave every hydrogen outside.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Propene. (b) C3H6. (c) Three carbons with a double bond between the first two, 2, 1 and 3 hydrogens along the chain. (d) A functional group is the reactive group in a molecule; the alkenes' is the C=C double bond.

steps.working: C2H4 + H2 → C2H6. The product is ethane.
steps.decision: Two hydrogens add, one to each carbon, so the alkene becomes the alkane of the same length. A nickel catalyst is used, but the equation is what carries the marks.

steps.working: C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH. The product is ethanol.
steps.decision: Write steam, not water: Summer 2024's report names water as the commonest wrong answer for the reagent, even though the formula is the same.

options: Because the reaction is run with the water as a gas, at high temperature and pressure
Because water and steam are different compounds
whyMenu.explain: Same substance, different state. The conditions need it as a vapour, and the scheme asks for the word steam.

steps.working: One of the two bonds between the carbons opens, leaving each carbon with a spare bond.
steps.decision: Say that one bond of the two opens, not that the bond breaks: the carbons stay joined.

steps.working: One atom or group from the small molecule joins each carbon, so nothing is left over and only one product forms.
steps.decision: That is what makes it addition rather than substitution: there is no second product.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) C2H4 + H2 → C2H6, giving ethane. (b) C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH, giving ethanol. (c) One of the two bonds between the carbons opens, and one atom or group joins each carbon, so there is only one product.

(a) Describe a test that would tell them apart, and give the result for each. [3]

steps.working: Shake each gas with bromine water.
steps.decision: Name the reagent exactly: bromine water, not bromine. Saying what you do with it is part of the mark.

steps.working: With ethene the bromine water is decolourised: orange to colourless.
steps.decision: Give both colours. 'It goes clear' is refused: clear is not a colour, and the scheme prints colourless.

steps.working: With ethane there is no change: it stays orange.
steps.decision: A test needs both results, or it does not tell anything apart. The negative result is a mark of its own.

steps.working: Complete combustion gives CO2 and H2O: C2H4 + O2 → 2CO2 + 2H2O before balancing the oxygen.
steps.decision: Carbons first, then hydrogens. Two carbons give 2CO2; four hydrogens give 2H2O.

steps.working: The products hold 2 × 2 + 2 = 6 oxygen atoms, so 3O2: C2H4 + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 2H2O.
steps.decision: Balance the oxygen last. Counting one O2 per carbon gives 2 and leaves the water unbalanced.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Shake each with bromine water: ethene decolourises it from orange to colourless; ethane leaves it unchanged. (b) C2H4 + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 2H2O.

items.stem: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
items.skill: Prerequisite from c2-homologous-series-alkanes; you are not expected to have met the alkenes yet

options.feedback: The alkanes. This lesson's family has two hydrogens fewer, and keeping the two rules apart is most of the difficulty.
That is the family this lesson is about. The alkanes carry two more hydrogens.
No family on this specification has that formula; for butane it would give four hydrogens instead of ten.

items.stem: How many covalent bonds does a carbon atom form?

options.feedback: Four, whether they go to four different atoms or two of them go to the same one, as in a double bond.
Oxygen forms two. Carbon forms four, which is why a double bond still leaves two bonds free on each carbon.
It never changes. Counting to four at every carbon is how you check a structure you have drawn.

items.stem: What does a double line between two atoms in a displayed formula mean?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.4 — reading a structure

options.text: the two atoms share two pairs of electrons
options.feedback: A double bond. It uses two of each carbon's four bonds, which is why an alkene has fewer hydrogens.
The lines are bonds, not molecules. Two lines between the same pair of atoms is one double bond.

options.text: the bond is twice as long
options.feedback: A double bond is actually shorter and stronger, but what the two lines record is two shared pairs.

items.stem: What is the general formula of the alkenes?

options.feedback: Double the carbons and stop. The +2 belongs to the alkanes.
That is the alkanes. An alkene has two hydrogens fewer, because the extra C–C bond uses two bonding positions.
That is the alcohols, which carry an OH group and contain oxygen.
For ethene that would give two hydrogens; it has four.

items.stem: An alkene has three carbon atoms. What is its name and molecular formula?
items.skill: Name and write the formula of an alkene

options.feedback: Prop for three carbons, -ene for the double bond, and 2 × 3 hydrogens.
Ethene has two carbons. Summer 2025 records this exact substitution when candidates named an alkene from its structure.
The name is right but the formula uses the alkane rule. An alkene is CnH2n, so 2 × 3 = 6.
But- means four carbons. Count the chain before choosing the prefix.

items.stem: A question asks you to circle the functional group in a molecule of propene. What should the circle contain?

options.text: the two carbons and the double bond between them
options.feedback: The C=C and nothing else. That is what the group is.

options.text: the two carbons, the double bond and the hydrogens on them
options.feedback: The hydrogens are not part of the group, and Summer 2025 records the mark being lost for exactly this.
Then the circle says nothing: the point is to pick out the reactive part.

options.text: the carbon at the end of the chain
options.feedback: A single carbon is not a functional group. The alkenes' group is the double bond between two of them.

items.stem: Why are the alkanes less reactive than the alkenes?
items.skill: Link reactivity to the functional group

options.feedback: No reactive spot. Every reaction in this topic happens at the alkenes' C=C.
Chain length varies in both families and has nothing to do with it.
They do carry two more hydrogens, but the reason is the missing functional group, not the hydrogen count.
The first four of both families are gases. State has nothing to do with reactivity here.

items.stem: An unknown gas decolourises bromine water. What does this show?

options.text: it contains a carbon-to-carbon double bond
options.feedback: The test is for C=C, which means the gas is an alkene.
An alkane leaves bromine water unchanged. Decolourising it is the positive result.
Bromine water is not an indicator. It tests for the double bond.
The test says nothing about oxygen; it reacts with the C=C.

items.stem: Which description of the bromine-water colour change would the scheme accept?
items.skill: State the colour change in full

options.feedback: Both ends of the change, and colourless rather than clear.
Clear is not a colour: a milky solution can be clear of lumps. The scheme prints colourless.
Two problems: no starting colour, and clear instead of colourless. Give both ends of the change.
That runs it backwards. Bromine water starts orange and loses its colour.

items.stem: Ethene reacts with steam. What is the product?

options.feedback: The H and the OH add across the double bond, giving the alcohol.
Ethane comes from adding hydrogen, not steam.
That is an oxidation product further along; steam gives the alcohol.
Those come from burning it. Addition keeps every atom in one product.

items.stem: What happens to the double bond during an addition reaction?

options.text: one of the two bonds opens and a new atom joins each carbon
options.feedback: The carbons stay joined by a single bond, and nothing is left over.

options.text: both bonds break and the molecule splits
options.feedback: That would be cracking. In addition the molecule stays in one piece and grows.

options.text: the double bond stays and the atoms join the hydrogens
options.feedback: The double bond is the reactive spot; it is what opens.

options.text: a hydrogen is replaced by the new atom
options.feedback: That is substitution, which is what alkanes do. Addition makes one product and nothing else.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist chemical terms used widely and accurately; organised with clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.

indicativeContent.point: Shake a sample of each gas with bromine water.
The ethene decolourises the bromine water, orange to colourless.
The ethane leaves it unchanged: it stays orange.
Ethene is an alkene, unsaturated, with a carbon-to-carbon double bond.
That double bond is the alkenes' functional group: the reactive group in the molecule.
The bromine adds across the double bond, which is why the colour disappears.
Ethane is an alkane and has no functional group, so it does not react.

scheme.for: a banded answer covering the test and the chemistry behind it: shaking each gas with bromine water, the orange-to-colourless change with ethene and no change with ethane, ethene being unsaturated with a C=C functional group, the bromine adding across that bond, and ethane having no functional group
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Method first, then both results, then why.
One word in the colour change is refused every year.
parts.workedSolution: Shake a sample of each gas with bromine water. The ethene decolourises it: the orange colour changes to colourless. The ethane leaves it unchanged, still orange. Ethene is an alkene and is unsaturated, because it contains a carbon-to-carbon double bond, and that double bond is the alkenes' functional group — the reactive group in the molecule. The bromine adds across the double bond, which is why the colour disappears. Ethane is an alkane with no functional group, so it does not react and the bromine water keeps its colour.

findTheMistake.stem:
Méabh is asked: 'Give the reagent and the result of the test for a carbon-to-carbon double bond. [2]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The reagent is right. The result is not, for two reasons: it gives no starting colour, and it uses the word clear. The scheme prints orange to colourless, and refuses clear every year, because a solution can be clear and still be coloured.
correction: The bromine water changes from orange to colourless.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the two marks: bromine water is right and stands. Give both ends of a colour change, and use colourless rather than clear. Those five words — orange to colourless — are worth writing out once and reusing.

findTheMistake.stem:
Odhrán is asked: 'An alkene has four carbon atoms. Give its molecular formula, and name the functional group of the alkenes. [2]'
His answer:
studentWorking: The functional group is the carbon-to-carbon double bond.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The functional group is right. The formula uses the alkane rule: CnH2n+2 would give ten hydrogens, but an alkene is CnH2n, so four carbons give eight. C4H10 is butane, not an alkene at all.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the two marks. The functional group stands. The formula needs the alkene rule: double the carbons and stop. Write both general formulae at the top of the page before you start — they are one character apart and cost marks every year.

His answer:

The first line is the one that goes: the reaction is run at high temperature and pressure, so the water is present as steam, and the scheme asks for that word. Summer 2024 records water as the commonest wrong answer here.

findings.asked: The reagent that converts ethene into ethanol, the name of that product, and a drawn addition product.
findings.wentWrong: Water was given instead of steam; the name ethanol was often missing; the drawn addition product was poor.
findings.rule: Ethene plus steam gives ethanol; one atom or group joins each carbon of the former double bond.

insight.ruleToRemember: Alkenes are CnH2n and unsaturated, with a C=C functional group: circle that bond and nothing else. Bromine water goes orange to colourless with an alkene and is unchanged with an alkane — colourless, never clear. Addition opens one of the two bonds and joins an atom or group to each carbon: bromine gives C2H4Br2, hydrogen gives ethane, steam gives ethanol.
insight.aStarSignal: Drawing an alkene of any length with the double bond in the position its name gives, and writing all three addition equations with the right product and the word steam.
